name: Urochloa
common_group: Signalgrasses — dense, spreading, and big-spikelet comparisons
look_here_first: SIGNALGRASS: first find raceme branches bearing OVOID, TWO-FLORET spikelets. Then collect mature units and compare SPIKELET SIZE and SHORT LOWER GLUME: U. reptans tiny (1.5–2.2 mm; glume ~1/8–1/4); U. fusca plump and intermediate (2.4–3.4 mm; glume ~1/4–1/3); U. texana distinctly larger (4.5–5.9 mm; glume ~half to two-thirds). Head tightness and branch radiating angles vary; do NOT identify by silhouette or call a native/introduced species without measured ripe spikelets. Detailed Texas signalgrass check: don't confuse the whitish hairy collar with the 1–1.8 mm ciliate membranous ligule. Whole panicles alone can't identify the large 4.5–5.9 mm U. texana without its actual 2.4–3.2 mm lower glume and mature hard wrinkled upper fertile lemma. Upper branches may hold paired spikelets or one surviving member of an aborted pair. Measure several from one source-vouchered plant.

priority: Whole panicle with attached racemes as an orientation clue, not final ID
At least five intact ripe spikelets matched to a 1-mm ruler
Compare lower glume in lateral view as fraction of an intact whole spikelet
Inspect 2-flowered spikelet: lower sterile/staminate floret and firm fertile upper lemma
Check ligule/collar and rooted basal stems ON SAME plant; branch spread or common name alone is not proof

comparison_lesson.title: Three signalgrasses — photograph head, then measure the spikelet
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: SMALL reptans 1.5–2.2 and tiny lower glume; MEDIUM fusca 2.4–3.4 and short lower glume; BIG texana 4.5–5.9 and half-length lower glume. All measurements in mm on ripe spikelets.
quick_split: BROWNSEED SIGNALGRASS: start with a tallish branching head of multiple usually ascending spikelet-bearing racemes, then look for plump blunt obovoid spikelets (roughly 2.4–3.4 mm depending source). Lower glume is relatively short, commonly about ONE-QUARTER to ONE-THIRD of the whole spikelet. The existing flowering photograph supports the clustered head, not the glume proportions; confirm on ripe material with a millimeter scale.

CREEPING SIGNALGRASS: source-labelled photo shows multiple slender radiating racemes with tiny crowded spikelets. Verify 1.5–2.2 mm ripe spikelets and their extremely short lower glume (about 1/8–1/4). In vegetative material, seek real lower STEM NODES rooting on the soil—do not infer rooted creeping stems from an isolated seedhead photograph.

TEXAS SIGNALGRASS: the new close-up now shows multiple ASCENDING branches lined with comparatively large elongate green spikelets (about 4.5–5.9 mm in UT records). On a separately collected ripe spikelet, lower glume typically reaches about HALF to TWO-THIRDS of spikelet length. Don't turn a CC-licensed photo or wide grass clump into confirmed glume lengths without a ruler.
guardrails: All three canonical species preserved; former Brachiaria/Panicum name combinations are not new cards.
Head compactness is not decisive: U. reptans may have 5–15 rather closely spaced racemes bearing crowded PAIRS of tiny spikelets even when branches spread.
Ripe size estimates from Kew and UT vary slightly by flora (fusca Kew 2.4–3 vs UT 2.9–3.4), so compare multiple measured spikelets rather than hard borderline rules.
The new Texas panicle closeup documents attached large-looking ovoid spikelets, NOT actual mm length or lower glume ratio. The new fusca vegetative image does NOT show a flowering head.
Original photo rights include CC BY-NC and new Wikimedia CC BY / CC BY-SA. Per-panel credits, NC restrictions and ShareAlike retained.
County-native range checks remain paused; don't change any existing taxonomy/range claims or insect metrics.

what_to_teach_crew: Start with a true flowering branch and two-flowered SPIKELET, not the common name 'signalgrass'.
Compare head architecture, but NEVER make a native versus introduced call solely on compact versus radiating branches.
Use a one-millimeter ruler: mature U. reptans typically 1.5–2.2 mm, U. fusca 2.4–3.4 mm, and U. texana 4.5–5.9 mm; if near boundary, dissect glumes.
Identify the tiny CLASPING LOWER GLUME at the base of an intact spikelet and compare its fraction of total spikelet length; don't count it as the hardened upper fertile lemma.
U. reptans sometimes roots from lower nodes: prove by photographing ACTUAL roots, never infer it from a common name.
Comparative photos: first three original locally archived species photos, one licensed Texas panicle close-up and one licensed greenhouse U. fusca vegetative view.
Former Brachiaria/Panicum combinations can refer to same taxon. Preserve documented nativity and HOLD status without a separate BONAP audit.
Texas signalgrass: physically lift the blade to expose a true short ciliate membrane separate from white collar hairs; take a 1-mm photo, don't mark an outer-sheath tuft as a ligule.

Texas signalgrass: beneath the 4.5–5.9 mm attached whole spikelet examine a ~2.4–3.2 mm basal glume vs almost full-size upper glume; distinguish lower male floret from hard ridged upper fertile lemma.
Texas signalgrass: a missing second spikelet on the branch may mean developmental abortion; one observed spikelet doesn't rule out this species. Photograph multiple nodes.

visual_comparison.title: UROCHLOA — three installed species, five real licensed comparison photo panels
visual_comparison.subtitle: Original three taxon-labelled photo files plus one useful CC BY 4.0 Texas panicle closeup and one CC BY-SA 4.0 vegetative fusca comparison. No glume anatomy falsely arrowed. Texas signalgrass reference is now a true local canonical JPEG, not just a Wikimedia hotlink. Two real U. texana USDA seed-lab images now SHOW comparative glume faces and separated fertile lemma/true grain with millimeter ticks; they are NOT pictures of U. fusca or U. reptans.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: SMALL reptans 1.5–2.2 and tiny lower glume; MEDIUM fusca 2.4–3.4 and short lower glume; BIG texana 4.5–5.9 and half-length lower glume. All measurements in mm on ripe spikelets.

items.label: Existing Brownseed signalgrass photo
items.image_role: Original physically stored and pixel-inspected species-labelled photograph; IDs remain based on the credited source determination
items.caption: Visible 1-photo original has clear dense flowering branch cluster and nearby broad leaf, but does not resolve individual spikelet glumes.
items.why_it_matters: Native Texas signalgrass candidate with a TIGHT upright cluster of thick, short flowering branches carrying many blunt, plump 2.4–3 mm spikelets. Compare mature spikelet SIZE AND SHAPE, and small lower glume (~one-quarter to one-third of spikelet) with U. texana and U. reptans. The current image shows the tight head and broad blade, NOT glume structure.
items.creator: Minnette Marr
items.photo_status: EXISTING ORIGINAL JPEG INSPECTED; only obvious visible structures arrowed; collar/glume/lemma anatomy not certified from photo; rights and creator retained.

items.label: Existing Creeping signalgrass photo
items.image_role: Original physically stored and pixel-inspected species-labelled photograph; IDs remain based on the credited source determination
items.caption: Photo shows only slender radiating flowering branches and small spikelets in a grass-rich background; does NOT show the creeping stem base or any glume.
items.why_it_matters: Introduced in many Texas floras. Look for an annual with decumbent or creeping rooted stems and a LOOSE spreading/ascending set of slender flowering racemes (unlike dense blunt-headed U. fusca). Measure a tiny ~1.5–2.5 mm ovoid spikelet and look for the almost missing basal glume; a seedhead photo alone does not show rooted basal nodes.
items.creator: Wen-Hsiang Cheng
items.photo_status: EXISTING ORIGINAL JPEG INSPECTED; only obvious visible structures arrowed; collar/glume/lemma anatomy not certified from photo; rights and creator retained.

items.label: Existing Texas signalgrass photo
items.image_role: Original physically stored and pixel-inspected species-labelled photograph; IDs remain based on the credited source determination
items.caption: Whole-plant original shows broad grass leaves and flowering stems amid other grasses; no individual spikelet/glume anatomy resolves, so arrows intentionally avoid species-diagnostic claims.
items.why_it_matters: Native Texas signalgrass with comparatively BIG ovoid pointed spikelets (~4.5–6 mm), borne singly or in pairs along several ascending side branches of a terminal panicle. Check the lower glume (around half to two-thirds of spikelet length), cross-veined lower lemma and tough, transversely wrinkled upper fertile lemma. Whole-plant overview alone is not enough for confirmation.

items.label: TEXAS SIGNALGRASS — identifiable panicle and visible spikelets
items.image_role: Additional verified Commons close-up of the fertile panicle; unlike original wide landscape, this photo resolves individual green spikelet contours, but not dissected lower glumes
items.caption: Real source-labelled panicle photographed by Sam Kieschnick. Several ascending spikelet-bearing branches and comparatively bulky ovoid green spikelets are visible. Photo has NO 1-mm scale; lower glume length, vein number and fertile lemma cannot be confirmed from the intact head.
items.why_it_matters: Closes the largest original Texas signalgrass visual gap: learn what a fertile head actually looks like before taking a measured mature spikelet for a safe native-vs-introduced identification.
items.creator: Sam Kieschnick
items.photo_status: PHYSICALLY ARCHIVED: exact Sam Kieschnick Commons CC BY 4.0 panicle JPEG, decoded and source-hashed. Gross branching/spikelets visible; no ruler, no individual lower glume, no ligule or 2-floret dissection. PROVISIONAL — USER PHOTO REVIEW PENDING.
items.modification_note: JPEG RGB encode/resize, stripped EXIF/GPS; original photograph subject unchanged. HTML arrows are independent overlays.

items.label: 7 · ACTUAL FLORETS and CARYOPSES — A/B florets, C/D grains, mm ruler
items.image_role: 7 · ACTUAL FLORETS and CARYOPSES — A/B florets, C/D grains, mm ruler
items.caption: USDA original Urochloa TEXANA A/B true mature florets dorsal and ventral side; C/D detached caryopses ventral and dorsal. A correctly oriented real millimeter scale runs beneath these units. The reddish/hardened floret is not a second species; pale grain C/D is the caryopsis after removing its envelopes. There is no demonstrated true leaf ligule in this image.
items.why_it_matters: Separates hard fertile lemma/palea from caryopsis and outer glumes. Do NOT teach that the two grains are multiple florets in the same intact spikelet.
